title: Define it
hookLine: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, as it is (Meditations 3.11)

lines: A WORRY ARRIVES AS A CLOUD.
cards: A worry rarely arrives in plain words. It arrives as a cloud. Something about money.
Something about that test result. Something about the way she said goodnight. It's big and blurry and fills the room.
Now try writing it down in one flat sentence, the way a clerk would. Sometimes the cloud shrinks the moment it has edges. Marcus Aurelius used this trick on himself, and wrote down how it works.

teach.h: MAKE A DEFINITION OF EACH THING.
teach.b: Book three's eleventh entry calls this one more aid to add to the others. Always make a definition, or a description, Marcus writes, of whatever presents itself to your mind.
See what it is in substance, stripped bare, whole, and tell yourself its name and the names of the parts it's made of.
His point is that what upsets us is often less the thing than the coat we put on it. A late bill becomes I'm failing at life. A curt email becomes they're about to fire me.
Defining strips the coat off. A late bill is a piece of paper asking for an amount by a date. That may still be a problem, but now it's one you can see.

teach.h: WHAT IS IT, WHAT DOES IT ASK OF ME?
teach.b: Then he asks of each thing: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last, and what does it ask of me? Gentleness, courage, truth, faithfulness, simplicity? A defined thing points to a response.
A cloud just points to dread. Nothing so enlarges the mind, he says, as being able to examine everything that happens methodically and truly.
Look at what this week has built. While I can. Could I say it.
Keep faith. Judge carefully. Only this.
And now, as it is. Seven short lines, each small enough to say in one breath.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.11 by writing a worry down in one plain sentence, naming what it is and what it asks of them, before deciding how to respond.

o: looking up the dictionary meaning of every word you hear
deciding firmly what you believe and never changing it
describing a thing plainly, stripped bare, before reacting to it

games.q: as it is — tap the pairs.
p: what we add to the bare thing
what does it ask of me?

s: Marcus says to describe things in vivid, emotional terms
he says to see them stripped bare, and name them and their parts.
Marcus asks of each thing how long it will last
it's one of his questions, with what it is and what it asks of me.
Marcus says defining things plainly makes the mind smaller
he says nothing so enlarges the mind as examining things methodically and truly.

games.q: on the drive to work, your car starts making a new grinding noise. your mind fills with storm clouds. what fits 3.11?
o: imagine every way it could go wrong.
describe it plainly: a new noise, from the front, when braking.
turn up the radio and ignore it.
games.why: Marcus defines the thing bare: a noise, with a place and a time. what it asks of you, for now, is a call to a mechanic and some patience.

practice: Bring up one worry that's been sitting with you, and let it be a cloud for a moment.

Then describe it in one flat sentence, as a clerk would, with no adjectives and no predictions: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last? Last, ask Marcus's question, what does it ask of me, and notice its size now.

wordCard.voice: Define it. Marcus's method: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, name it and its parts, and ask what it asks of you. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'appearance, impression': in Stoic language, what presents itself to the mind before we judge it.

carryVoice: Your line: as it is. A thing with edges is a thing you can meet. A full week, done.
